A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CapeLLM. All 14 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables and appendices A–C, are readable and support comparison. Retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original MP-100 benchmark results, architecture and instruction ablations, and additional output-format and pre-training experiments in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and appendix results and adds experiments on training strategies, cumulative inference, input robustness and decoding, plus qualitative density analyses.

M1.justification: v2 adds dynamic-round training with variable numbers of keypoints per conversation and cumulative inference that carries earlier keypoint prompts into subsequent predictions (Sections 3.3 and 4.3). These extend the procedure substantially. The fixed-round grouping, DINOv2–LLaMA architecture and three-decimal coordinate representation already existed in v1.

E1.justification: MP-100 and its category coverage remain unchanged. v2 expands evaluation scenarios to train–test description mismatches, including removed or placeholder descriptions, and explicitly examines several occlusion conditions. These extend input-condition coverage without introducing another dataset or pose-estimation task.

E2.justification: GraphCAPE-S and CapeX remain the benchmark comparators. v2 newly evaluates a LocLLM-style training control in Tables 3–4. Figure 5 also introduces a ground-truth-centered, fixed-variance Gaussian as a qualitative reference distribution.

E3.justification: New experiments compare training strategies under single versus cumulative inference, vary description substitution, test resolutions through 336×336, and evaluate seven decoding strategies. The original benchmark splits and default training settings remain. Separately, the stated Hiera token count changes from less than 20% of other encoders' tokens to 20% fewer; no changed implementation or rerun is established.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic analyses: cumulative reasoning, training-strategy controls, vague and missing descriptions, resolution sensitivity, decoding alternatives, occlusion cases and predictive-density comparisons (Tables 3–9; Figures 4–5). Earlier instruction, backbone and pre-training ablations largely survive in the appendices rather than being removed.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly visualizes predictive uncertainty using multiple decoded samples and kernel density estimation. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests for benchmark scores. The new density visualization does not establish uncertainty in reported PCK averages.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including dynamic-training PCK@0.2 of 96.05 with single inference versus 97.28 with cumulative inference, and LocLLM-style mPCK of 84.00 versus fixed-round 91.98. Existing benchmark split scores remain unchanged; Table 2 corrects the query-only average from 91.60 to 92.60. Several retained appendix tables omit previously reported intermediate PCK thresholds.

T1.justification: v2 adds Equation (6), a digit-wise conditional probability factorization, and a cited claim that decoding represents a truncated conditional density at resolution 10^(-K). v1 described coordinate encoding without this formal distributional argument. No new proof is supplied within v2.

C1.justification: v2 expands the main contributions to dynamic-round training, cumulative spatial reasoning and flexible probability-distribution modeling. It also strengthens novelty positioning to the first fully support-free CAPE framework. The claim of outperforming prior five-shot methods was already present in v1 and is not itself a new contribution.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantive mechanism explanations: dynamic training enables accumulated relational context to help prediction, and decoded distributions can better respect object boundaries than fixed-variance Gaussians. It also interprets new experiments as evidence of robustness to description, resolution and decoding variations. These extend v1's explanations concerning descriptions, backbone tuning and model size.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository hyperlink and decoding parameters such as temperature, top-k and nucleus thresholds. However, it omits v1's explicit split-1 ablation scope, padding rule for incomplete keypoint groups, and some pre-training data and initialization details. Default optimizer, hardware and training-budget disclosures remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around LocLLM as the closest approach, distinguishes CapeX's skeletal dependence, and connects CapeLLM to chain-of-thought and decoding-based regression. Table 1 changes CapeX's support-free designation from a checkmark to a partial-status triangle. New references support these arguments, while the Long-CLIP citation is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, related-work discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The experimental narrative is reorganized around cumulative reasoning and distribution modeling, while much of v1's main-text ablation discussion moves into an expanded Appendix B. Author affiliation and contact formatting also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 2 to depict coordinate-token decoding, adds occlusion and density figures, and removes v1's qualitative name-variation figure. It adds experimental tables, splits the earlier combined ablation table into separate appendix tables, reduces columns in several retained tables, and relocates the description table and instruction diagrams.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of CapeLLM's adaptation: Tables 3–4 add the missing LocLLM-style training control and reveal when cumulative inference helps or hurts. New stress tests examine reliability beyond v1's name-variation example, while the benchmark average is corrected and code access is documented. Some reproducibility details are lost and the distribution claims remain qualitatively evaluated, but the stronger controls and diagnostic evidence provide a substantial net improvement.
